claims.text: A light microscope forms an image with visible light focused by glass lenses (objective then eyepiece); it can be used on living or stained specimens and gives a colour image, but its resolution is limited to about 0.2 µm (200 nm), so useful magnification stops at about ×1500.

claims.text: An electron microscope forms an image with a beam of electrons focused by electromagnets in a vacuum; because the wavelength of an electron beam is far shorter than that of visible light it resolves far smaller structures, but the image is black and white and the specimen is dead and prepared (dehydrated, fixed and treated with heavy metals).

claims.text: In a transmission electron microscope the beam passes through a very thin section and gives a two-dimensional image of the internal structure, with a resolution of the order of 1 nm; in a scanning electron microscope the beam scans the metal-coated surface and gives a three-dimensional image of the outer surface, with a lower resolution of the order of several nanometres.

claims.text: Resolution is set mainly by the wavelength of the radiation used: the shorter the wavelength, the smaller the distance between two points that can still be seen as separate, which is why an electron microscope (about 1 nm) resolves far finer detail than a light microscope (about 200 nm).

claims.text: Enlarging an image further, for example by photocopying a photomicrograph, raises the magnification but not the resolution: structures already blurred together stay blurred, so no more detail is revealed (empty magnification). It is the microscope, not the image, that has a resolution.
